summary: Paul Gilbert, a tech lead at Arista Networks based in New York City, presents to AI executives about building self-managed AI network infrastructure. He focuses on the "plumbing" — training and inference infrastructure — rather than agents or applications. Gilbert explains the two-network AI architecture: backend networks (completely isolated, connecting GPUs at 400Gbps via leaf-spine topology) and frontend networks (for storage access). He describes the H100 server with 8 GPU ports and 4 Ethernet ports, emphasizing unprecedented traffic levels. Key differences from traditional data centers include no oversubscription (1:1 bandwidth ratio), entirely new bursty synchronized traffic patterns, and the fact that a single GPU failure can halt an entire training job. Power requirements shift dramatically from 7-15kW racks to 100-200kW water-cooled racks. Gilbert covers RoCEv2 congestion control (ECN for gradual flow control, PFC for emergency stops), load balancing challenges (traditional 5-tuple entropy fails for GPU traffic; Arista uses bandwidth-percentage-based and collective-aware cluster load balancing achieving ~93% utilization), and the scale of bandwidth — 4.8 terabytes per H100 server, with 800Gbps approaching and 1.6 terabytes expected by end of 2025 or early 2027. He details Arista's EOS features: lossless Ethernet with tuned buffer allocation matching model packet sizes, RDMA packet capture for diagnosing dropped packets, an AI agent loaded on Nvidia GPUs that communicates with switches to verify PFC/ECN configuration and provide GPU-side statistics for correlating GPU vs. network problems, and smart system upgrade allowing switch code upgrades without taking switches offline. Gilbert emphasizes network isolation, BGP as the preferred protocol, EVPN/VXLAN for multi-tenancy, and the importance of visibility and telemetry to detect problems before developers call. He references cluster designs: a 1,400 GPU cluster with 800G leaf-spine links and 400G to GPUs, and a 4,000 GPU cluster using Arista 7800 series 16-slot switches (576 800G GPUs per box). He concludes by mentioning the Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC), with version 10 expected to be ratified Q1 2025, shifting more intelligence into NICs and simplifying network forwarding, with products expected Q3-Q4 2025. Job completion time is the key metric — if it degrades, the network is likely the problem.

takeaways: AI networks require isolated backend networks for GPUs at 400Gbps with 1:1 bandwidth ratios — no oversubscription — unlike traditional data centers built at 1:3 or 1:10 ratios
H100 servers generate 4.8 terabytes of traffic per server; 800Gbps is current, with 1.6 terabytes on the network expected by end of 2025 or early 2027
Power requirements shift from typical 7-15kW racks to 100-200kW water-cooled racks; a single H100 server with 8 GPUs draws 10.2kW
Traditional 5-tuple entropy load balancing fails for GPU traffic; Arista uses bandwidth-percentage-based and collective-aware cluster load balancing achieving ~93% uplink utilization
Arista's AI agent loads on Nvidia GPUs to verify PFC/ECN configuration with switches and provide GPU-side RDMA statistics, enabling correlation of GPU vs. network problems
Smart system upgrade allows switch code upgrades without taking switches offline — critical for networks with thousands of GPUs and 64+ switches
RDMA packet capture snapshots dropped packets with headers and error codes, diagnosing why packets were dropped rather than silently discarding them
Buffer allocation tuned to model packet sizes is a win-win since buffering is expensive in switches; models send and receive particular packet sizes
Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC) version 10 expected ratified Q1 2025, shifting congestion control and packet spraying intelligence into NICs; products expected Q3-Q4 2025
Job completion time is the key operational metric — degradation from 1 hour to 4 days likely indicates a network problem; checkpoints help but are expensive

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.summary: Paul Gilbert introduces himself as an Arista Networks tech lead focused on AI and data center infrastructure. He frames his presentation around the 'plumbing' of AI — training and inference infrastructure — rather than agents or applications. He references Dr. Wed Sosa's slide showing training vs inference GPU requirements and notes that Chain of Thought and reasoning models are changing inference patterns.

sections.title: AI Network Architecture: Backend vs Frontend
sections.summary: Gilbert explains the two-network AI architecture: backend networks (completely isolated, connecting GPUs at 400Gbps via leaf-spine topology) and frontend networks (for storage access). He describes the H100 server with 8 GPU ports and 4 Ethernet ports, emphasizing this traffic level is unprecedented in enterprise networking. Networks use simple protocols (iBGP/eBGP) and are built for 24x7 operation.

sections.title: Scale, Hardware, and Software Differences
sections.summary: Covers scale up vs scale out (customers buy 8-GPU servers that can't be expanded; scale out via network), hardware/software differences (CUDA, NCCL collectives shape traffic), and how AI applications differ from traditional web/app/database workloads — GPUs all communicate synchronously and one failure can fail the entire job.

sections.title: Bandwidth, Load Balancing, and Traffic Patterns
sections.summary: Details the massive bandwidth (4.8TB per H100 server, 9.6TB for 800Gbps), no oversubscription design, bursty synchronized traffic patterns, and load balancing challenges. Traditional 5-tuple entropy fails for GPU traffic (single IP); Arista uses bandwidth-percentage-based balancing achieving 93% utilization. Also covers GPU failure and cable/transceiver reliability issues at scale.

sections.title: Power, Cooling, and Congestion Control
sections.summary: Covers the dramatic power shift from 7-15kW racks to 100-200kW water-cooled racks (H100 server draws 10.2kW), bidirectional traffic patterns (east-west GPU at wire rate, north-south storage calmer), and RoCEv2 congestion control combining ECN (gradual end-to-end flow control) and PFC (emergency buffer-full stop).

sections.title: Network Isolation, Telemetry, and Arista EOS Features
sections.summary: Gilbert elaborates on complete backend isolation — no DMZs, firewalls, or internet connections like traditional data centers. He stresses that model failures generate different operational calls than traditional app failures. He advises speaking with data scientists about models being built since they affect network design. He covers Arista EOS features: lossless Ethernet with ECN/PFC, buffer tuning matched to model packet sizes (buffering is expensive), RDMA packet capture that snapshots dropped packets with headers and error codes, an AI agent loaded on Nvidia GPUs that verifies PFC/ECN configuration with switches and provides GPU-side RDMA statistics for correlating GPU vs. network problems, and smart system upgrade allowing switch code upgrades without taking switches offline.

sections.title: Design Principles, Cluster Examples, and Ultra Ethernet
sections.summary: Gilbert reiterates no oversubscription on the backend, point-to-point SL3/31 addressing (IPv6 optional), BGP as preferred protocol, EVPN/VXLAN for multi-tenancy, and collective-aware cluster load balancing. He shows a 1,400 GPU cluster (800G leaf-spine, 400G to GPUs) and a 4,000 GPU cluster using Arista 7800 series 16-slot switches (576 800G GPUs per box). He describes three networks: backend (GPUs), frontend (storage), and inference deployment. He introduces the Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC), version 10 expected ratified Q1 2025, shifting congestion control and packet spraying into NICs. He concludes emphasizing job completion time as the key metric and that checkpoints are expensive.

limitations: AI networks are completely new to enterprise network engineers; configuring GPUs took hours initially
Traditional 5-tuple entropy load balancing fails for GPU traffic due to single IP addresses
Storage vendors cannot currently match GPU backend traffic levels
Cable and transceiver problems are significant at thousand-GPU scale
Single GPU failure can stop entire training job; checkpoints help but are expensive
Air cooling is impossible for AI racks; water cooling required
Network has no visibility into GPUs without the AI agent; GPU-switch configuration mismatch on PFC/ECN can cause disasters
Buffering is an expensive commodity in switches
Models can checkpoint but checkpoints are really expensive
Ethernet hasn't fundamentally changed in ~30 years; UEC needed for better congestion control, packet spraying, and NIC-to-NIC communication
